senses: An enthusiast of films and the cinema.
ety: Borrowed from French cinéphile, equivalent to cine- + -phile.
examples: The gulf between cinephiles and the public has grown wide. There are pictures that make a lot of money, but seldom win big Oscars or attract young people to the show

senses: The knowledge, acquired through meditation, that one's self (atman) is identical with Ultimate Reality (Brahman).
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit ज्ञान (jñāna, “knowledge”).
examples: Jnana is a direct knowing of things as they really are.

senses: A stock exchange.
Any place, real or imagined, where the value of a thing is settled.
A meeting of stamp collectors and/or dealers, where stamps and covers are sold or exchanged.
ety: Borrowed from French bourse, from Old French borse, from Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa). Doublet of purse, compare Danish børs, Swedish börs, German Börse. See also bursar.
examples: In brief, Le Chiffre plans, we believe, to follow the example of most other desperate till-robbers and make good the deficit in his accounts by gambling. The 'Bourse' is too slow.
Euronext, the first euro-zone crossborder bourse, makes its debut
For quotations using this term, see Citations:bourse.

senses: A fennel cultivar with a bulb-like structure at its base, used as a vegetable; Florence fennel (Foeniculum vulgare var. azoricum).
ety: Borrowed from Italian finocchio (“fennel; (derogatory) male homosexual”). Doublet of fennel and finook.
examples: Finocchios are shoots of the fennel, an odoriferous plant of the Umbelliferae family.
For the first time, finocchio, or Florence fennel, has performed for me as it should and has swollen out into bulbous protrusions at the base of its leaf stalks.
The strong anise odor of finocchio repels many insects from other vegetables.

senses: Sounding sorrowful, mournful or melancholic.
ety: From Middle English pleintif, plentyff, from Old French pleintif (“aggrieved, lamenting”) (whence modern French plaintif), from plainte (“lament, complaint”); see plaint. Doublet of plaintiff.
examples: I can see by your plaintive smile something is wrong, so spill it.
When my wife and I heard a plaintive whinny from our laundry room the other day, we knew that our old dryer had cycled its last load.

senses: The philosophy or ethos of trying to achieve balance in one's life.
ety: Borrowed from Swedish lagom (“just right”).
examples: Lagom seems to be fighting a losing battle against a world run by the instant gratification of social media, where we all want to be seen and be heard.
The typical Scandinavian home is the very essence of lagom. It's neither too sparse nor too fussy, neither overly minimalist nor overdone.
Not surprisingly, lagom extends to our cuisine as well – the Swedes take great pride in eating healthily, drawing on their own cooking traditions and the seasons' offerings.

senses: A small green and yellow European finch, Carduelis spinus spinus or Carduelis spinus, now Spinus spinus.
ety: From dialectal German Sisschen, Zeischen, diminutive form of Middle High German zīsec, apparently ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čižь (compare e.g. Polish czyżyk).
examples: I sat there on a bench in dappled shade, beside an aviary full of brightly feathered finches and siskins fluttering about.

senses: A child prodigy; a wonderchild.
A highly talented or gifted person, especially one who is successful at a young age.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German Wunderkind, from Wunder (“wonder”) + Kind (“child”). Compare native wonderchild.
examples: The downfall of Austria’s onetime political Wunderkind put a spotlight on the cozy, sometimes corrupt, relationship between right-wing populists and parts of the news media.
When the verdict comes down, the transformation of the wunderkind founder of Theranos from black-clad genius to besuited milquetoast will be an integral part of the story.

senses: Men's clothing (and accessories), particularly in a retail context.
ety: From men + -s- + -wear.
examples: Derek Guy was a relatively unknown menswear writer with 25,000 followers on Twitter in 2022.

senses: Befitting of a royal court; reflecting the manners or behaviour of people at court; stately, rich or fine, and so suitable for a royal court.
ety: From Middle English courtly, equivalent to court + -ly.
examples: He swept off his hat and made a deep courtly bow.
The troubadours sang songs about courtly love.
You have too courtly a wit for me; I’ll rest.

senses: Tending to give orders to others, especially when unwarranted; domineering.
ety: From boss + -y.
examples: Over in the wardrobe department a bossy woman in ill-fitting dungarees tried to talk her into wearing a short red low-cut dress for the test.
Cuphead is a difficult gauntlet through a ton of bosses, from evil clowns to bossy queen bees.

senses: Characteristic of a curmudgeon; churlish.
ety: From curmudgeon + -ly.
examples: In A League of Their Own (1992), as the shouty baseball coach to an all-girls team, he's once again a curmudgeonly but lovable mentor figure.
Since Swift and Kelce debuted their relationship early in the season, certain (curmudgeonly) NFL fans grumbled over the numerous camera shots of the singer’s private box.

senses: Sweetened, with, or as if with, honey.
Sugary, syrupy.
Dulcet or mellifluous.
ety: From Middle English honyed; equivalent to honey + -ed.
examples: There were no honeyed words from Dr. Beeching to mollify Scottish feeling on rail service closures during his one-day visit in May.

senses: The character of being social; sociability
The quality of an animal kind of being social.
Social events or entertainments; pleasantries.
ety: From social + -ity, from French socialité or directly from Latin sociālitās (“fellowship, sociality”), from sociālis (“social”), from socius (“companion, ally”) + -ālis.
examples: To understand how sociality is programmed—that is, how friendships are programmatically organized and shaped, let us consider the ways in which the platform simulates existing notions of friendship.

senses: Having or characterized by gnarls; gnarled.
ety: From gnarl (“knot in wood”) + -y. The slang senses were particularly popularized by US surf culture in the 1970s.
examples: Out of one window I can see the garden, those mysterious deep-shaded arbors, the riotous old-fashioned flowers, and bushes and gnarly trees.

senses: A covered walkway, with open sides, that connects two buildings.
ety: From breeze + way.
examples: One of his favorite pastimes was strolling through the breezeway on warm spring afternoons.
If you are on a higher level and can't get to a lower apartment, hunker down in the breezeway of the apartment building

senses: To use a trephine during surgery.
To perforate with a trephine.
ety: Borrowed from French tréphine, from Latin trepanum, from Ancient Greek τρύπανον (trúpanon, “auger, borer”). Doublet of trepan.
examples: The pony was cast, and trephined, a middle-sized trephine (or bone saw) being used, which removed a circular piece of bone about the size of a two shilling piece, from the face immediately over the air cavity.

senses: A hand printing tool, in the US often a roller, used to spread a thin even layer of ink. Early brayers, consisting of a vertical cylinder with a single handle, were designed to break up thick inks before spreading.
One who brays, or makes the sound of a donkey.
ety: From bray + -er.
examples: Sound forth my Brayers, and the welkin rend

senses: A small box or tin (can) with a lid for holding dried tea leaves used to brew tea.
A (usually small) box, chest, or tin with a lid, and often with partitions, used to keep things in.
A small lidded bin for food waste.
A movable tray or other mechanism for holding (sometimes within a piece of equipment or machinery), securing, and transporting a removable component.
A lightweight wheeled cart; specifically, one attached to a bicycle as a conveyance for a child, or pulled by hand and used to transport groceries away from a shop.
ety: An alteration of catty (“(unit of) weight used in China, equivalent to 1⅓ pounds avoirdupois (about 0.605 kilograms)”), borrowed from Malay kati (“weight used in China, Indonesia, and Japan”), from Tamil கட்டி (kaṭṭi, “measure of weight; clod, lump”), from கட்டு (kaṭṭu, “to coagulate, congeal, or consolidate (into a concretion); to harden”).
examples: A sauce caddy brought with the tacos offers a choice of salsa cruda, a thin puree of tomatillos, and an emulsion of red chilies.
Place the disc in the DVD caddy.

senses: Hard and insular; resistant to change.
ety: From scler(a) + -otic.
examples: Most state parties--Democrat or Republican--are sclerotic and dutiful, and little help to local candidates.
His funeral ends the era of first generation leaders in post-colonial Asia, in fact in the world, with the exception of a few sclerotic kleptocrats mostly in Africa.

senses: A soft biscuit or cookie prepared with almond or coconut dough.
ety: From French macaron. Doublet of macaron.
examples: I will take charge of the cake department, including, if I remember rightly, plum and plain, rout cakes, and macaroons, finger biscuits, and cracknels.

senses: Not having shaved; not shaven; untrimmed.
ety: From un- + shaven.
examples: He was an unshaven little man in a threadbare coat like a gaberdine, with his feet in slippers, and I thought him a harmless fool.
When Handy had gone, Bert Barricue sagged in, unwashed, unshaven. He sat down stiffly.

senses: A Wellington boot.
Force on a pedal or increase to any fuel or power for an engine or motor.
Force or effort.
ety: Clipping of Wellington boot + -y.
examples: Dad has great big welly boots. For squishing in the mud; Two great big black welly boots: Thud, thud, thud.
Come on! Put some welly into it!

senses: Dirty or grimy.
Disreputable; sleazy.
ety: Probably a blend of scummy + fuzzy 1960s, US, colloquial, expressive coinage, with influence from scum, fuzzy, lousy, sleazy.
examples: I’d been counting on Paul, a scuzzy-but-still-sexy manager of a music club in Shoreditch, to meet up with me on my first night in London.

senses: Any of a class of German mercenaries of the 15th and 16th centuries, most of whom were pikemen and foot soldiers.
A gambling card game in which the dealer is given an initial card and the players another; cards are then turned up until the value (rank) of one of those cards is met.
ety: Borrowed from French lansquenet, from German Landsknecht, from Lands (“of the land”) + Knecht (“servant”). Doublet of Landsknecht.
examples: One could see part of the dimly lit court where under an enclosed poplar two soldiers on a stone bench were playing lansquenet.
And so it was over the game of lansquenet that I scored my first triumph.

senses: A device used to suppress ("snub") voltage transients in electrical systems, pressure transients in fluid systems, or excess force or rapid movement in mechanical systems.
ety: From snub + -er.
examples: Ground teams have now begun instructing the primary mirror segments and secondary mirror to move from their stowed-for-launch configuration, off of snubbers that kept them snug and safe from rattling from vibration.

senses: The wood just under the bark of a stem or branch; it differs from the heartwood in color and in physiologic activity (flow of sap).
ety: From sap + wood.
examples: A popular myth is that sapwood is not as strong as heartwood.

senses: A drink made with yogurt diluted with water and flavoured with salt or fruit juice.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani लस्सी / لسی (lassī).
examples: Karam stirred his lassi as if trying to unchurn the yoghurt.

senses: Someone or something that feels.
Something ventured to test another's feelings, opinion, or position.
ety: From Middle English feler, feeler, felar, equivalent to feel + -er. Animal organ definition from 1660s. Transferred sense of "proposal put forth to observe the reaction it gets" is from 1830.
examples: Are you more of a feeler or more of a thinker?
I sent out some feelers but they didn't seem interested.
This survey is designed to get a feeler about how the citizens feel about the proposed new highway.

senses: A small wicker-covered clay pot containing hot coals, worn under clothing in Kashmir to warm the skin.
ety: Borrowed from Kashmiri کانٛگٕر (kāngụr).
examples: Under the phiran her little kangri of hot coals sent long fingers of heat across her stomach.

senses: Someone who systematically obstructs the actions of others.
Someone who attempts to impede the progress of legislation.
ety: From obstruction + -ist.
examples: The obstructionists didn't have their own plan, but they counted, successfully, on delay to frustrate any alternative.

senses: Contained in the whole an integral number of times, a factor or divisor.
ety: From French aliquote, from Latin aliquot.
examples: The United States standard yard … has a thin strip of silver, ¹⁄₅ inch broad, let into it through its entire length. It is divided into small divisions, each being an aliquot part of an inch.

senses: A member of various legendary races of dwarfs, or supernatural peoples of diminutive stature.
ety: From Latin Pygmaeī, from Ancient Greek πυγμαῖος (pugmaîos, “a member of a legendary race of dwarves”), from πυγμή (pugmḗ, “fist (as small as a fist)”). In Ancient Greek, first mentioned by Homer; only applied to actual human races in the 19th century.
examples: I've seen unicorns in Burma and a yeti in Nepal; / and I've danced with ten-foot Pygmies in a Montezuma Hall.

senses: The advocacy of a revision of some accepted theory, doctrine or a view of historical events.
ety: From revision + -ism.
examples: Tories spent last week boldly whistling their unique brand of the kind of historical revisionism that has played a major part in getting us here.
As for Jones’s performance as Mandy Cohen, it united two leading facets of the funnyman’s repertoire: his fondness for female impersonation, and his passion for historical revisionism.
Meanwhile, Holocaust survivors are dying every day. There are few left to protest the new revisionism.

senses: An ethnographic study drawing on one's own anecdotal or personal experience, or an approach to conducting research in which anecdotal or personal experience is foregrounded.
ety: From auto- + ethnography.
examples: The aborigine's autobiography was also an autoethnography. It told much about the culture he grew up in.

senses: Tending to boast or brag.
ety: From Middle English bostful, equivalent to boast + -ful.
examples: He wrote a boastful autobiography, recording all his great deeds.
It makes one's blood boil, yet heart tremble, to think that we Englishmen and our American descendants, with their boastful cry of liberty, have been and are so guilty

senses: Using ethnographic techniques to describe one's own life, or events in which one is a participant.
ety: From auto- + ethnographic.
examples: At the same time it often resorts to free indirect speech rather than dialogue, frequently using an autoethnographic point of view, suggesting a more personalized mode of shared ethnographic documentation.

senses: A hormone, related to serotonin, that is secreted by the pineal gland, and stimulates colour change in the skin of reptiles, and is involved in the sleep and wake and reproductive cycles in mammals.
Any material similar in its chemistry and effect to the natural hormone.
ety: From mela- + tone + -in, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black, dark”).
examples: How exactly melatonin relates to sleep is still not understood.
Melatonin production can be delayed or arrested by even brief flashes of bright light entering the eye, research has shown.

senses: A type of fine powder, as of sandarac, or cuttlefish bone, sprinkled over wet ink to dry the ink after writing or on rough paper to smooth the writing surface.
Charcoal dust, or some other coloured powder for making patterns through perforated designs, used by embroiderers, lacemakers, etc.
ety: From French ponce, from Latin pūmex. Doublet of pumice.
examples: At the Thorn, or at a meagre kitchen table, or even on the carpenter’s workbench, he spreads open the portfolio, lights a candle stub, slices a fresh quill, and arranges pounce pot and ink well.

senses: An aeroplane route.
An elevated road.
Synonym of skybridge: an elevated corridor connecting buildings above ground level.
ety: From sky + way.
examples: Iʼd taken to swinging past the fourth floor skyway at random intervals.
